draft.title: Relative frequency
card: A trial is one go at an experiment, such as one roll of a die. An event is an outcome you are counting, such as rolling a 6.
Relative frequency = number of times the event happened ÷ number of trials. It can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

Example: Sam flips a drawing pin 50 times and it lands point up 30 times. Relative frequency = 30 ÷ 50 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%. Past data works too: if 12 of the last 40 days were rainy, the estimate is 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3.
Use relative frequency when outcomes are not equally likely, like the drawing pin, so counting outcomes cannot give the probability. More trials usually give a better estimate.
draft.remember: Relative frequency = times it happened ÷ total trials. More trials usually give a better estimate.

a.q: Mia spins a spinner 40 times. It stops on red 14 times. What is the relative frequency of red?
a.why: Relative frequency = 14 ÷ 40 = 0.35. The tempting option 14/26 divides by the number of non-red spins, but the total number of trials must go on the bottom.
a.clue: Divide by the total number of spins.

b.q: Lena flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Ravi flips the same coin 500 times and gets 270 heads. Whose estimate of the probability of heads is likely to be better?
opts: Ravi's 270/500, because it uses more trials
Lena's 7/10, because it is a higher value
Lena's 7/10, because she suspects the coin is unfair
Both are equally good, because it is one coin
b.why: More trials usually give a better estimate of probability, so Ravi's 270 ÷ 500 = 0.54 is likely closer to the true value. Lena's 7/10 = 0.7 comes from only 10 flips, so luck can change it a lot. Using the same coin does not make a short run as reliable as a long one.
b.clue: With only a few flips, how much can luck change the result?

b.best: Ravi's 270/500, because it uses more trials
